cases.title: Static on Pier Nine
cases.tagline: A pledge night, a pirate broadcast, and a fired DJ everyone wants to blame.
cases.role: You volunteer one night a month as the signal analyst for KPIR 91.3, Pier Nine Radio. The station runs Google SecOps. You have read access to Search and nothing else.
opening: Pledge Night at Pier Nine Radio is the one night the station's phones never stop. At 03:10, between a jazz block and the overnight news, the playout system aired a segment nobody scheduled: a distorted voice reading the names of the night's biggest donors, one by one, followed by forty seconds of static.

By 03:14 the board treasurer, Hal Brunner, was in the control room. By 03:20 he had a suspect: Marco Vela, the overnight host the station let go last week, who still knows every password on the pier. Station manager Odalys Reyes is not ready to call anyone. 'Bring me what the logs say,' she tells you. 'Not what the room thinks.'
The station's events are in Google SecOps. You have until the morning news to work out what happened, in what order, and who needs to be told.

cases.summary: Pledge Night. A pirate segment airs at 03:10, the board has a suspect, and the logs say something else.

cases.title: The week after
cases.tagline: The password is reset, the task is gone, the range is blocked. Did the fix hold, and is the path one story?
cases.role: You are back at the signal desk for the membership drive, one week after Pledge Night. Odalys applied every item on your Contain and Eradicate lists. You still have read access to Search and nothing else.
cases.summary: One week later, at the same station, after the fix. Subtler, quieter, and the question is whether the fix held; then, on Monday, whether the events are one story and who owns the hosts they touched.
opening: Friday, 18:00, the membership drive. The pledge-desk password was reset on Saturday morning, the PledgeSync task and its folder were removed, AUTOMATION-01 was rebuilt, and the gateway now blocks 203.0.113.0/24. Dez also wrote an allowlist of sponsor domains before lunch, by copying every sponsor-looking name out of last week's logs, so the station could tune out the known-good and see what was left.

Nothing airs that should not. No burst of failures, no encoded PowerShell, no forty-eight-megabyte upload. At 05:40 Odalys asks the only question that matters a week after an incident: did the fix hold? She wants it answered the way last week's brief was answered: from the records, with the records.
The station has twelve hours of its own logs again. The attacker, if they came back, had a week to read the same brief you wrote.

On Monday morning the ticket is still open. Before it closes, Odalys wants two things the Friday brief could not give her: proof that the gateway login and the file server are one story, written as a query someone can rerun, and the station directory beside every row, so each item of the fix has an owner.

people.name: Odalys Reyes

people.name: Hal Brunner

people.name: Priya Nair
people.note: Second drive. Also received this week's lure; did not open it.

systems.name: The allowlist

systems.name: The directory
systems.note: The station's entity context: users with titles, roles and remote access, assets with owners and criticality, each record valid over a time range. See the Entities panel on the desk.

boundary: Everything here is fiction: the station, the people, the logs, the addresses. Nothing runs against a real SIEM. Do not type real workplace values into this site; practise the shape of the query here and use real values only inside tools your employer authorizes.
